traps.name: 5-phenylpent-1-en-5-ol
traps.why: Number from the end that gives the -ol the lowest locant: the OH is on C1, the alkene on C4.

productDistractors.why: You reduced the C=C as well. NaBH₄ only delivers hydride to the polarised C=O; an isolated C=C is untouched. Getting both needs H₂/Pt.
This reduced the wrong π bond. NaBH₄ is a hydride nucleophile and needs an electrophilic carbonyl carbon; it does not add to an isolated C=C at all.
NaBH₄ does react here: a ketone is exactly what it reduces. 'No reaction' would be right for an ester or an isolated alkene, not for a ketone.
Removing the oxygen completely is Clemmensen (Zn(Hg)/HCl) or Wolff–Kishner chemistry. A hydride adds H to the carbonyl carbon and leaves the oxygen behind as OH.

routeDistractors.why: H₂/Pt reduces the C=C too and gives the saturated alcohol. To touch only the ketone you need a hydride (NaBH₄).
PCC is an oxidant (alcohol → aldehyde/ketone). You are going the other way: ketone → alcohol needs a hydride.

explanation: NaBH₄ reduces the ketone to a 2° alcohol and leaves the isolated C=C alone. The carbinol carbon is a new stereocenter made from an achiral ketone, so the product is racemic.
tip: Mild hydride, one job: carbonyls only. The alkene is just along for the ride.

productDistractors.why: The ester does not stay in one piece. After the first hydride adds, ethoxide is expelled from the tetrahedral intermediate, so the OEt can never end up bonded to the benzylic carbon as an ether.
A single hydride does not give a stable hemiacetal. The tetrahedral intermediate expels ethoxide to give benzaldehyde, which LiAlH₄ reduces again.
Right idea to split the ester, but LiAlH₄ never stops at the aldehyde: benzaldehyde is more reactive than the ester and is reduced to benzyl alcohol straight away.

routeDistractors.why: NaBH₄ is too mild for an ester: nothing happens. Esters need LiAlH₄, then a water workup.
H₂/Pt reduces C=C and aldehyde/ketone C=O; in this course esters survive hydrogenation. Use the hydride.

explanation: Two hydrides add to the acyl carbon: the first gives a tetrahedral intermediate that expels ethoxide (benzaldehyde + ethoxide), the second reduces the aldehyde. After the H₂O step you hold benzyl alcohol AND ethanol.
tip: An ester always falls apart under LiAlH₄: count two alcohols on your clipboard.

traps.name: heptane-2,6-dione
traps.why: Carbon 1 has only one carbon neighbour, so it is an aldehyde (-al), not a second ketone.

traps.name: 2-oxoheptanal
traps.why: The aldehyde carbon is always C1, so the ketone sits on C6, not C2.

productDistractors.why: HIO₄ is an oxidative cleavage: each carbinol carbon ends up at the carbonyl level. If you drew alcohols, no oxidation happened and the C–C bond would still be intact.
The CH–OH carbon had one carbon neighbour and one H, so it becomes an aldehyde, not a methyl ketone. Only the carbon that carried the CH₃ becomes a ketone.
That is what PCC would do to the 2° alcohol. HIO₄ does not oxidise an alcohol in place; it cleaves the C–C bond between the two OH-bearing carbons.
Periodate cleavage stops at the aldehyde. Going on to the carboxylic acid is Jones/chromic acid chemistry, not HIO₄.

routeDistractors.why: PCC oxidises the 2° alcohol to a ketone and leaves the 3° alcohol and the ring intact. Cleaving the ring between the two OHs is HIO₄'s job.
O₃ cleaves C=C double bonds. There is no alkene here; a vicinal diol is cleaved by HIO₄.

explanation: HIO₄ breaks the C1–C2 bond of the diol. C1 (bearing CH₃) has two carbon substituents → ketone; C2 (bearing H) has one → aldehyde. The ring opens into a single seven-carbon chain: 6-oxoheptanal.
tip: Cut between the two OHs, then count carbons on each cut end: two C's → -one, one C → -al.

productDistractors.why: You nitrated the ring. NaNO₂/acid is nitrous acid, which reacts with the NH₂ group itself (diazotisation); it never adds NO₂ to a ring C–H. That needs HNO₃/H₂SO₄.
This is the diazonium salt, the intermediate after step 1. You still need H₂O and heat to replace N₂ with OH.
NH₂ was swapped for NO₂. Nitrous acid converts NH₂ into N₂⁺, which leaves as N₂ gas; the OH from water takes that carbon. NO₂ is never involved.

routeDistractors.why: HNO₃/H₂SO₄ is nitration: it adds NO₂ to the ring and leaves NH₂ where it is. To swap NH₂ for OH you need the diazonium salt: NaNO₂/H₂SO₄ cold, then H₂O and heat.
Diazotisation must be done at 0–5 °C: aryl diazonium salts decompose as soon as they warm up. Keep the ice bath on for step 1.
You made the diazonium salt and stopped. Step 2 (H₂O, heat) replaces N₂ with OH.

explanation: NaNO₂/H₂SO₄ at 0–5 °C converts the NH₂ into a diazonium group; H₂O and heat then replace N₂ with OH on the same carbon. The methyl group is untouched: 4-methylphenol.
tip: Nitrite, not nitric: NaNO₂ talks to the amine, HNO₃ talks to the ring.
source: Carey 12e §24 phenol prep via diazonium (toolkit P1); seeded Missed

routes.why: tert-Butoxide is hindered but that does not matter for the nucleophile; CH₃I has no β-hydrogens and is a perfect SN2 electrophile.
Methoxide is a strong base and tert-butyl bromide is 3°: E2 wins and you get 2-methylpropene, not the ether. Put the bulky group on the alkoxide side and use CH₃I.

choices.label: A 2°/3° halide with an alkoxide gives E2 (an alkene), not SN2
SN2 can't happen on an aryl carbon
AlCl₃ is not a base, so no alkoxide forms
The alkyl halide was added before the base

explanation: In a Williamson synthesis the alkoxide can be as hindered as you like, but the halide must be CH₃ or 1°. Route A pairs tert-butoxide with CH₃I (SN2 fine); route B pairs methoxide with a 3° bromide (E2).
tip: Bulky alkoxide, tiny halide. Never the other way round.
